Welcome back! This week you'll use what you learned in the previous labs in a data analysis exercise. Our question: how are income and CO2 emissions related across countries? We'll answer it with data from [Our World in Data](https://ourworldindata.org/).

We will:

- import data, select variables and deal with missing values with `dplyr` (Lab 1)
- join two datasets (Lab 7)
- use a regular expression to keep only certain rows (Lab 5)
- make plots with `ggplot2` (Lab 9)
- reshape data with `pivot_longer()` (new)
- fit and test a prediction model with `tidymodels` (Lab 8)


# The data

The datasets come from the [OWID CO2 repository](https://github.com/owid/co2-data) and its [world regions page](https://ourworldindata.org/world-region-map-definitions).

The `data` folder contains:

- `owid_emissions.csv`: emissions and energy data, plus many other variables
- `owid_gdp_population.xlsx`: GDP and population
- `owid_co2_codebook.csv`: variable definitions, units and sources
- `owid_regions.csv`: a country-to-region lookup

### 4C. Distribution

Now we want to plot both distributions side by side with `facet_wrap()` (Lab 9). `facet_wrap()` makes one panel for each value of a column. To use it with our data, we need both values, GDP and CO2, in one column.

With `pivot_longer()` we can reshape our data frame. It makes the data longer, with more rows and fewer columns. It takes three arguments.

- `cols` sets the columns to pivot, here `gdp_per_capita` and `co2_per_capita`.
- `names_to` names the new column that stores the old column names.
- `values_to` names the new column that stores their values.

Here is an example with made-up data. Run it and compare the two tables.

```{r}
example <- tibble(
  country = c("A", "B", "C"),
  gdp_per_capita = c(1000, 1000, 1000000),
  co2_per_capita = c(1, 3, 15)
)

example

example |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = c(gdp_per_capita, co2_per_capita),
    names_to = "variable",
    values_to = "value"
  )
```

Each country now appears twice, once per variable. The old column names, `gdp_per_capita` and `co2_per_capita`, are now values in the new `variable` column. Their numbers are in the new `value` column. We could now use `facet_wrap()` to make one panel per variable. To learn more, see the [pivoting chapter in R for Data Science](https://r4ds.hadley.nz/data-tidy.html#sec-pivoting).
